query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The native oxide layer present on as‐received Q235 steel governs its corrosion resistance during both room‐temperature and high‐temperature (700–900 °C) aggressive salt exposure. Specifically, when this pre‐formed oxide evolves under annealing, it develops into a continuous, dense, and adherent protective film that retards salt-induced degradation, whereas its removal or degradation during annealing leads to enhanced corrosion and mass loss.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its as-received condition with its native, naturally formed surface oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Systematically remove the native oxide from one set of samples (via chemical etching or mechanical polishing) and preserve it on another set, then subject both groups to controlled annealing at 700–900 °C under inert conditions, followed by exposure to an aggressive salt environment.
generation.conditions: Test at room temperature (ambient exposure) versus high-temperature (700–900 °C) in aggressive salt atmospheres; the protective effect is expected only when the native oxide is preserved and appropriately evolved during annealing under the high-temperature regime.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity, density, and adhesion of the evolved oxide layer formed during annealing.
generation.mechanism: The pre-existing native oxide layer either thermally stabilizes into a protective barrier that limits salt access and elemental dissolution or, if removed/disrupted, fails to form a coherent scale. In the preserved state, annealing promotes diffusion and re-oxidation that produces a dense, adherent oxide film which acts as a diffusion barrier against corrosive species.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples that retain their native oxide layer are predicted to show lower mass loss, fewer microstructural signs of salt penetration, and improved corrosion resistance relative to samples where the oxide has been removed prior to annealing, especially under high-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel samples with unaltered native oxide layer, showing moderate corrosion resistance at room temperature and enhanced protection after optimal annealing.
generation.boundary: The mechanism is expected to be significant under aggressive salt exposure at high temperatures (700–900 °C) where oxide scale formation/deterioration is accelerated; at ambient conditions where corrosion kinetics are slower, the effect of the native oxide evolution may be less pronounced.
generation.uncertainty: The precise influence of additional factors such as impurity levels, microstructural heterogeneities, or secondary phases formed during annealing on the oxide evolution and its protective properties is not fully resolved.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of Q235 steel samples: one group in which the native oxide layer is chemically removed and another group left with the native oxide intact. Subject both groups to identical annealing conditions (e.g., 800 °C in an inert atmosphere for a fixed period) and subsequently expose them to an aggressive salt environment (e.g., molten salt) at 700–900 °C. Characterize the samples by measuring weight loss, performing microstructural cross-sectional analysis (e.g., SEM), and assessing the continuity and composition of the oxide scale (e.g., XPS or EDS).
measurements: Microstructural integrity of the oxide layer (via SEM imaging)
Chemical composition and adhesion of the oxide scale (via surface analytical techniques)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis would be falsified if there is no significant difference in corrosion degradation (i.e., similar weight loss, oxide integrity, and salt penetration) between the oxide-preserved and oxide-removed sample groups under high-temperature salt exposure.

cited_evidence.text:
Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

Development of materials suitable for molten fluoride salt environments started in the 1950s with the Aircraft Reactor Experiment (ARE) [4] . This experiment used Inconel 6

decision.trend: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels mainly reported empirical performance improvements under aggressive salt exposure—hardness, wear resistance, and mass-change metrics—without isolating the mechanistic origin of protection. More recent work on HEAs, especially in high-temperature corrosive environments, has begun to correlate microstructural features (such as oxide film formation, elemental depletion, and phase transformations) with hot-corrosion behavior. However, no study so far has controlled the key variable of the pre‐existing surface oxide on a common steel such as Q235, despite indications that oxide layer evolution during annealing might dictate protection persistence or failure.
decision.unsolved: The causal mechanism by which the native oxide layer on Q235 steel—potentially altered by subsequent annealing—governs corrosion resistance over both room-temperature and high-temperature (700–900 °C) regimes remains unresolved. It is unclear how the properties (e.g., density, composition, and adhesion) of the preformed oxide determine the development or failure of protective behavior in aggressive salt environments, and in which conditions this effect is operative.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the pre-treatment of Q235 steel to either remove or preserve its native oxide layer, then apply controlled annealing (at 700–900 °C) in both inert and aggressive salt atmospheres. Key parameters would include annealing temperature, time, and controlled atmosphere to isolate the evolution of the protective oxide layer.
decision.why: This next step builds directly on the trend from performance-based studies toward mechanistic investigations by isolating the role of the native oxide. It tests the hypothesis that the initial oxide’s evolution (stabilization or degradation) under annealing controls corrosion behavior. The experiment’s design—with a clear reference (oxide-removed vs. oxide-preserved states) and sensitive conditions (room temperature vs. high temperature salt exposure)—addresses the gap highlighted by earlier studies, and an unexpected similarity in performance between the two states under high temperature would directly falsify the hypothesis.
